title: Lazy and concurrent collections
cards/0/body:
The object is expensive, it must be created once, and it is read all the time. Taking a lock on every read feels wasteful. Hence double-checked locking:

  • the first check is without a lock: the object exists — return it right away;
  • it does not — take the lock and check again: while we waited for the lock, another thread may have created the object.

Does this work without volatile? Under the general ECMA spec — no. In CoreCLR — yes: storing an object reference is a release, and a read through a reference honors data dependency (lesson 1). But only if the object is fully ready before the reference is written to the field.
cards/0/deep: For a singleton you usually need no double check at all. static readonly Settings Instance = Settings.Load(); — and the CLR itself guarantees the type initializer runs exactly once, under its own internal lock. The price is less control over when creation happens: without a static constructor the type is marked beforefieldinit, and initialization may happen before the first access.
cards/1/q: Another thread sometimes gets Settings with empty fields. Which line lets the object out before it is ready?
cards/1/explain: After this line the field is no longer null, and the first check in another thread lets it past the lock — to an object that is not loaded yet. Create and set up the object in a local variable, and write it to the field as the very last step.
cards/2/title: Lazy<T>: double-checked locking written for you
cards/2/body:
Lazy<T> stores a factory and calls it on the first access to Value. How it behaves under contention is set by LazyThreadSafetyMode:

  • ExecutionAndPublication (the default) — the factory runs under a lock, exactly once, other threads wait for the result;
  • PublicationOnly — no lock: several threads may run the factory at the same time, the first finished result lands in the field (via CompareExchange), the rest are thrown away;
  • None — no synchronization, for single-threaded objects. The fastest.
cards/3/title: Exceptions in the factory and LazyInitializer
cards/3/body:
A non-obvious behavior: if the factory throws in ExecutionAndPublication mode (or None), Lazy remembers the exception. Every later access to Value throws the same exception, and the factory is never called again. A network glitch at startup — and the object is "broken" until restart.

In PublicationOnly mode exceptions are not cached: the next access tries again.

If you do not want a separate Lazy object per field, there is LazyInitializer.EnsureInitialized(ref field, factory). Without an explicit lock it behaves like PublicationOnly: it checks the field for null and publishes the result via CompareExchange — just like the code from the Interlocked lesson.
cards/4/q: A Lazy<HttpConfig> in the default mode. On the first Value the factory threw HttpRequestException: the network was down. A minute later the network is up. What does the next Value access give?
cards/4/options/0: The same HttpRequestException: the exception is cached
cards/4/options/1: The factory runs again and returns the config
cards/4/options/3: InvalidOperationException: the Lazy is in a faulted state
cards/4/explain: ExecutionAndPublication caches the factory exception forever. If the failure can be transient — use PublicationOnly, your own retry code, or recreate the Lazy.
cards/4/wrong/1: Only PublicationOnly behaves like that. The default mode remembers the exception.
cards/5/q: Match the lazy initialization option with its behavior
cards/5/pairs/0/1: Factory under a lock, exactly one run
cards/5/pairs/1/1: The factory may run several times, the first result wins
cards/5/pairs/3/1: No Lazy object: a field and CompareExchange
cards/6/body:
ConcurrentDictionary is not a regular dictionary under a single lock.

  • Reads (TryGetValue, the indexer) take no locks: buckets are published so that a reader always sees a consistent state.
  • Writes take only the lock of their stripe (striped locking): an array of locks, each covering part of the buckets. Writers in different stripes do not interfere.
  • Operations over the whole dictionary — Count, Keys, Values, ToArray — take all locks at once. Calling them in a hot loop means stopping every writer.
  • A foreach is safe during concurrent changes, but it is not a snapshot: you may see some of the changes made during the enumeration.
cards/7/title: GetOrAdd and a factory that runs several times
cards/7/body:
GetOrAdd(key, factory) looks atomic, but the dictionary calls the factory outside the lock — so that slow or reentrant foreign code does not hold a stripe. Therefore:

  • several threads that miss the key at the same time will all run the factory;
  • one value ends up in the dictionary, and everyone gets exactly that one;
  • the other created values are simply thrown away — without Dispose.

For a cheap factory it does not matter. For an expensive one or one with side effects (a connection, a file, a paid request) you store not the value but a Lazy<T>. Extra Lazy objects cost next to nothing, and the factory inside the winning one runs once.
cards/7/deep: Same with AddOrUpdate: the dictionary also calls the update function outside the lock and repeats it on a race — it is a CAS loop over the value. So it must not contain side effects. There are GetOrAdd<TArg>(key, factory, arg) overloads: the argument is passed explicitly, the lambda captures nothing — no closure allocation per call.
cards/8/q: 10 threads call GetOrAdd with the same new key at the same time. What is true?
cards/8/options/0: The factory may run 1 to 10 times, but all threads get the same value
cards/8/options/1: The factory runs exactly once: GetOrAdd is atomic
cards/8/options/2: Each thread gets its own value, the dictionary keeps the last one
cards/8/options/3: Nine threads get an exception: the key was already added
cards/8/explain: The factory is outside the lock, so its runs are not limited. The insertion is under the stripe lock: the first insertion wins, the other threads see the key on the re-check and return the winner's value.
cards/9/q: Make the expensive connection open only once per key
cards/9/explain: Several threads may each create a Lazy object, but only one ends up in the dictionary, and everyone calls Value on it. The default ExecutionAndPublication mode guarantees a single Connection.Open. Remember the exception cache: a failed open stays in the dictionary — remove it with TryRemove.
cards/10/title: Lazy<Task<T>>: one load for everyone in async code
cards/10/body:
In async code the factory returns not a value but a Task. Put the task itself into Lazy: Lazy<Task<T>>. The first caller of Value calls LoadAsync and gets its task. Everyone else, even those who arrive at the same moment, gets the same task and awaits it — one task can be awaited any number of times. The Lazy lock is held only until the first real pause inside LoadAsync, while the method has not yet returned its task. The waiting itself happens with no lock and no busy threads.

The trap is the same as with cached exceptions. Lazy stores the task, not the result: if the load failed, a faulted task sits in it forever, and every later await throws the same exception. For transient failures the entry is removed from the dictionary in catch. The TryRemove(KeyValuePair) overload (.NET 5+) removes the entry only if the dictionary holds exactly this Lazy — and leaves alone a new one that another thread has already put in its place.
cards/11/q: The catch block was removed from the code above. The first load failed because of a transient network error. What do GetAsync calls get a minute later, when the network is back?
cards/11/options/0: The same exception: a Lazy with a faulted task sits in the dictionary forever
cards/11/options/1: A new load: the faulted task drops out of Lazy by itself
cards/11/options/2: AggregateException instead of the original exception
cards/11/options/3: InvalidOperationException: a task cannot be awaited twice
cards/11/explain: Lazy called the factory once, it returned a task, and the task faulted. Lazy keeps that task, and every await of a completed task immediately throws its exception. The catch with TryRemove removes the failed entry: the next call creates a new Lazy and starts the load again.
cards/11/wrong/2: await unwraps the task's exception and throws the original one, not AggregateException.
cards/11/wrong/3: A completed task can be awaited any number of times: each await immediately gets its result or exception.
cards/12/title: The other collections and the check-then-act trap
cards/12/body:
• ConcurrentQueue — no locks on the common path, array segments; the best choice for FIFO between threads.
  • ConcurrentStack — a linked list on a CAS loop, like the stack from the Interlocked lesson.
  • ConcurrentBag — each thread has its own list; it pays off when the same thread both adds and takes. As a general-purpose queue it is slower than ConcurrentQueue.
  • BlockingCollection — a blocking wrapper with a bounded capacity. In async code Channel replaces it.

The main trap: each operation is thread-safe, but their combination is not. if (!d.ContainsKey(k)) d[k] = v; — another thread gets in between the check and the write. You need one operation: TryAdd, GetOrAdd, AddOrUpdate, TryRemove, TryUpdate.
cards/13/options/0: Reading from a ConcurrentDictionary takes no locks
cards/13/options/1: Count on a ConcurrentDictionary is cheap: it reads one field
cards/13/options/2: Lazy in the default mode remembers the factory exception
cards/13/options/3: The GetOrAdd factory is called under the stripe lock
cards/13/options/4: ContainsKey followed by the indexer is not atomic, even on a ConcurrentDictionary
cards/13/explain: Count takes all the dictionary locks. The dictionary calls the GetOrAdd factory outside the lock on purpose, so it may run several times. Only a single operation is atomic, not a sequence of them.
